analysis.one_liner: Requires nursing homes to disclose their owners and finances, and ties Medicare and Medicaid payments to staffing and quality standards.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 6 cosponsors, never received a committee hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required nursing homes that bill Medicare and Medicaid to disclose who owns them, including hidden stakes in management companies, staffing agencies, and property firms they pay. Facilities that missed disclosure deadlines, or that failed a floor of 4.1 direct-care hours per resident per day, would have been publicly flagged and would have lost Medicare and Medicaid payment for new residents until they complied. It also would have created federal task forces to spot suspected payment misuse and refer it to inspectors general and the Justice Department, and funded $80 million in demonstration projects on person-centered care.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents and their families, who would get more information about who is behind a facility's care and who would be protected by a minimum staffing floor; taxpayers, who fund most nursing home care through Medicare and Medicaid and would gain a window into related-party deals that can drain money from care. Low-income facilities would also gain access to new demonstration grants.

how_it_helps.text: Would suspend Medicare and Medicaid payment for new residents at any nursing facility that fails to submit required ownership information within 30 days of the deadline, making disclosure a condition of getting paid.

Would require any owner with at least a 5% stake in a facility to disclose financial details — balance sheets, income statements, and cash flows — for any entity they own that contracts with the facility, and would require facilities to map out related companies including management companies, property companies, and outside parties paid more than $200,000.

Would establish a minimum standard of at least 4.1 direct-care hours per resident per day; facilities falling below it would be named on the public Care Compare website and would lose Medicare and Medicaid payments until they meet the standard.

Would create two federal task forces — a Data Liaison Team and an Interagency Board with the HHS Inspector General and the Justice Department — to identify common ownership patterns among poorly performing facilities, assess potential misuse of Medicare and Medicaid payments, and refer cases for investigation.

Would authorize $80 million for fiscal years 2023-2027 for demonstration projects on person-centered 'culture change' ($50 million) and information technology ($30 million), with one project's grants reserved for facilities serving a high proportion of Medicaid residents.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home owners and operators, who would bear the cost of compiling ownership disclosures, financial statements, and organizational charts, and who would risk losing Medicare and Medicaid payment — their primary revenue — for new residents if they missed deadlines or fell below the staffing standard. Indirectly, higher staffing and compliance costs could pressure facility finances and, if not offset by higher payment rates, taxpayer-funded Medicare and Medicaid programs.

drawbacks.text: The enforcement tool is blunt: suspending payment for new residents at a noncompliant facility could push a financially marginal home toward closure, and closing a nursing home displaces frail residents — often to facilities farther from their families.

The 4.1 direct-care-hours floor and the new disclosure requirements would impose real costs on operators at a time when many facilities, particularly those serving high shares of Medicaid residents, already operate on thin margins; unless Medicare and Medicaid rates rose to cover hiring, the standard could squeeze the very facilities that care for the poorest residents.

The oversight structure is bureaucratic: monthly task force reporting, a second interagency referral layer, and detailed financial submissions from owners would add administrative layers whose effectiveness depends entirely on future agencies actually enforcing them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents of a sector where ownership is often hidden behind layers of companies, the transparency and staffing provisions aimed at a real, documented problem, and the payment-suspension mechanism gave the rules teeth. The costs are genuine but modest relative to the stakes: compliance paperwork for owners, closure risk for the weakest facilities, and dependence on diligent enforcement. A well-designed version would pair the staffing floor with higher payment rates for facilities that need help meeting it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees the day it was introduced, and neither ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on July 29, 2022, joined by Rep. Mark Takano as the original cosponsor.
The same day, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee.
Six Democratic representatives cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
Neither committee held a hearing, markup, or vote, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home owners and investors are better off, because ownership and financial disclosure rules and the 4.1-hour staffing floor were never enacted; the existing disclosure system stays as it is.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, but the bill's entire support was Democratic — a sponsor, an original cosponsor, and 6 Democratic cosponsors, with no Republican backing.

industries.industry: For-profit nursing home owners and investors
industries.note: The bill would have stripped away anonymity in nursing home ownership, forcing anyone with a 5% or larger stake to file financial statements and to disclose related entities that contract with the facility. Owners who missed deadlines would have lost Medicare and Medicaid payment for new residents — the sector's main revenue.

industries.industry: Nursing home management, staffing, and property companies
industries.note: Related-party firms — management companies, property lessors, staffing agencies, food and supply vendors paid over $200,000 — would have had to be named in facility disclosures, exposing arrangements where facility money flows to affiliates of the owners. The Data Liaison Team would have specifically reviewed these payments for potential misuse of Medicare and Medicaid funds.

industries.industry: Nursing facilities with high Medicaid resident shares
industries.note: One of the two new demonstration projects would have reserved its grants for facilities serving a high proportion of Medicaid residents, directing $50 million toward person-centered 'culture change' at the facilities least able to fund it themselves.
